title: Right now: the first 24 hours after a fire
plain_summary: The first day decides how much of this claim can later be proven. Almost none of it is about insurance paperwork — it is about safety and evidence, in that order.

do_now.text: Wait for the fire department to release the building before going back inside.
do_now.why: Hot spots, carbon monoxide, and structural collapse are common causes of injury after fire crews leave the scene.

do_now.text: Record video of every room before anything is moved, cleaned, or thrown away — slow, narrated, drawers and closets opened.
do_now.why: This is the single most valuable evidence for the claim. Once cleanup starts, the pre-loss condition cannot be recreated.

do_now.text: Call the insurance company and get a claim number.
do_now.why: Under Fla. Stat. § 627.70132, notice of the claim starts the statutory clocks that require the insurer to respond by fixed deadlines.

do_now.text: Ask three questions on the first call: is there an advance for living expenses, what is the emergency-repair limit on the policy, and which companies is the insurer sending.
do_now.why: Each of these becomes a dispute later if it is never asked and never documented.

do_now.text: Write down the fire incident report number.
do_now.why: The report is usually a public record and can be requested later as evidence.

do_now.text: Remove documents and valuables if the fire department allows it — identification, passports, deeds, the insurance policy, medications, jewelry.
do_now.why: If investigators are still working the scene, they may escort removal and record what is taken, which also protects against later disputes.

do_now.text: Board up, tarp, and lock the property once it is released.
do_now.why: Securing the building after release is the owner's responsibility, not the fire department's or the insurer's.

do_now.text: Notify the mortgage company.
do_now.why: The mortgage company is a payee on every check the insurer issues and needs to be looped in early.

never_do.text: Do not let anyone remove, clean, or discard anything before video documentation exists.
never_do.consequence: The contents claim shrinks to whatever someone else happened to write down.

never_do.text: Do not sign anything a contractor hands over at the curb.
never_do.consequence: Curbside paperwork is a contract. It can create personal liability for whatever the insurance company does not pay.
never_do.reasonable_inaction: Declining every curbside offer, no matter how urgent it feels, is always the safer choice — there is no version of this where signing on the spot helps more than waiting a day to read it first.

never_do.text: Do not guess at dollar figures on the phone.
never_do.consequence: Early guesses get quoted back for the rest of the claim, sometimes for years.

never_do.text: Do not delay safety needs or medical care to finish a perfect video record.
never_do.consequence: No documentation is worth risking health or missing urgent care.
never_do.reasonable_inaction: If contents were destroyed beyond recognition, a shorter walkthrough is reasonable — there is little left to preserve by slowing down further to film it in full.

title: The first week: policy in hand, control over who touches the property
plain_summary: Two things matter this week: getting the actual policy in hand, and controlling who touches the property and belongings before anything is decided.

do_now.text: Request the complete policy in writing — declarations page, full form, and every endorsement, not the emailed summary.
do_now.why: The Homeowner Claims Bill of Rights gives a right to the full policy; the summary omits terms that end up controlling the dispute.

do_now.text: Start a claim log — date, time, who was spoken to, their title, what was said — and confirm anything important by email the same day.
do_now.why: Verbal agreements evaporate when a claim rotates between adjusters; a contemporaneous log is the only lasting record.

do_now.text: Keep every receipt for hotel, meals above normal spending, laundry, pet boarding, extra driving, and storage.
do_now.why: These are the additional living expenses the policy reimburses, and only the increase over normal costs counts.

do_now.text: Before signing any repair or cleanup authorization, write in a dollar cap, define exactly what work it covers, and cross out any clause assigning insurance benefits.
do_now.why: An unscoped authorization is a direct contract with the vendor for whatever insurance does not pay — and for policies issued on or after January 1, 2023, an assignment of benefits is void outright, so it buys nothing and only adds risk.

do_now.text: State in writing to the insurer that the property is now unoccupied because of the fire.
do_now.why: Many policies restrict coverage on vacant homes after 30 to 60 days; written notice on the record protects against a later vacancy denial.

never_do.text: Do not let a pack-out crew load a truck before an independent video exists and a written, item-level list from the crew is in hand.
never_do.consequence: Box-level entries like 'kitchen misc' become the ceiling on what gets paid for that box's contents.

never_do.text: Do not let anyone discard an item without written authorization and a photo.
never_do.consequence: An item nobody can prove existed cannot be claimed.

never_do.text: Do not give a recorded statement before reading the full policy.
never_do.consequence: A recorded statement gets compared line by line against anything said later, including at an examination under oath.

watch_for.signal: A letter arrives using the words 'reservation of rights'

title: The adjuster inspection and the clocks that start running
plain_summary: The adjuster represents the insurance company, not the policyholder. Being present, documenting independently, and getting an independent estimate protects the record from this point forward.

do_now.text: Be present for the inspection.
do_now.why: Scope decisions made without a witness are harder to dispute later.

do_now.text: Photograph everything the adjuster photographs.
do_now.why: A matching photo record prevents disputes over what was actually inspected.

do_now.text: Write down what the adjuster says is covered and email it back the same day.
do_now.why: A same-day written confirmation is evidence if the account of what was said changes later.

do_now.text: Get an independent repair estimate from a contractor chosen without the insurer's input.
do_now.why: The insurer's estimate reflects its own scope decisions; an independent estimate is the only check on it.

do_now.text: Ask for a copy of the field adjuster's report, not only the final estimate.
do_now.why: Comparing the field report against the final estimate costs nothing and surfaces a discrepancy if the scope changed between the two.

never_do.text: Do not treat the insurer's first written estimate as final.
never_do.consequence: An initial estimate is an opening position, not a determination of the full scope of covered damage.

watch_for.signal: The field adjuster's report describes more damage than the final estimate pays for

title: Documenting and inventorying belongings
plain_summary: Whoever writes the list controls what gets paid for it. This phase is tedious, unglamorous, and where the most money is typically lost by moving too fast.

do_now.text: Finish the independent room-by-room video before any pack-out truck is loaded.
do_now.why: Once contents leave the property, the household's own record is the only version of what existed.

do_now.text: Get the pack-out company's inventory in writing, item by item and not box by box, before the truck leaves.
do_now.why: A box labeled only with a general description becomes the ceiling on what that box's contents are worth.

do_now.text: Photograph the contents of each box as it is packed.
do_now.why: Box-level photos are the only record connecting a box label back to the specific items inside it.

do_now.text: Get a written non-salvageable list, agreed and photographed, before anything is disposed of.
do_now.why: Disposal without an agreed list removes the ability to dispute an item marked as a total loss.

do_now.text: Get the storage location, the right of access, the daily rate, and which coverage pays it — contents limit or additional living expenses — in writing.
do_now.why: Storage charges quietly consume one of two separate coverage limits, and it matters which one is being used.

do_now.text: Keep irreplaceable items out of the pack-out entirely.
do_now.why: Items that never leave the property cannot be lost, damaged, or disputed in a warehouse.

do_now.text: Build the item-by-item inventory: room, description, brand, model, serial number, quantity, age, original price, condition, and replacement cost today, with a source for that price.
do_now.why: This is the document the payment is calculated from — the level of detail in it becomes the level of detail in the check.

never_do.text: Do not agree to disposal of any item without a written authorization and a photo.
never_do.consequence: An item disposed of without agreement cannot later be claimed, however clear the damage was.

never_do.text: Do not accept an item returned as 'cleaned' that still smells of smoke without stating in writing that accepting it is not a waiver.
never_do.consequence: Silent acceptance can be read later as agreement that the item is no longer a covered loss.

never_do.text: Do not claim an item that was not actually owned.
never_do.consequence: Deliberate padding of the inventory is a felony, voids the entire claim, and hands the insurer a fraud theory to use against everything else on the list.
never_do.reasonable_inaction: Honest gaps and best-guess entries on a reconstructed list are normal and expected — nobody has perfect records after a fire, and noting uncertainty on an item is always safer than guessing with false confidence.

watch_for.signal: Storage bills keep climbing while the rebuild has stalled
An item returned as cleaned still smells of smoke

title: Understanding the payment: ACV, depreciation, and what Florida guarantees
plain_summary: Payment usually happens twice. Understanding why prevents two common, opposite mistakes: thinking a partial check means being underpaid, or thinking a partial check means being paid in full.

do_now.text: Track the actual cash value payment separately from recoverable depreciation, and keep in mind depreciation is released only after replacing items and sending receipts.
do_now.why: Insurers do not volunteer the second payment — it has to be requested with proof of replacement.

do_now.text: Ask in writing whether the policy includes building code upgrade coverage.
do_now.why: Current law deems this coverage included at 25 percent of the dwelling limit unless it was rejected in writing on an approved form, and code upgrades on an older home can exceed the cost of the repair itself.

do_now.text: Call the mortgage loss-draft department and ask for its checklist before mailing anything.
do_now.why: Every incomplete document packet adds one to two weeks to a staged disbursement.

do_now.text: Track both the dollar limit and the time limit on additional living expenses against the actual construction schedule.
do_now.why: Losing track of either limit separately from the other is the most common way this coverage runs out early.

never_do.text: Do not cash a check marked 'full and final settlement' without understanding it may close the claim.
never_do.consequence: Cashing that check can end the ability to recover anything more, even for damage discovered later.

never_do.text: Do not sign a release in order to get paid.
never_do.consequence: Nothing in the policy requires signing away rights in exchange for money that is already owed.

never_do.text: Do not assume the first offer is the final number.
never_do.consequence: A first offer is an opening position, and treating it as final forecloses negotiating the difference.

watch_for.signal: The home is a total loss and the insurer proposes anything less than the amount it was insured for

documents: proof of replacement receipts for depreciation
code-upgrade coverage election or rejection form

title: Rebuilding: supplements, contractor choice, and the living-expense clock
plain_summary: Demolition regularly exposes damage nobody could see before the original scope was agreed. That is normal, not a new claim, as long as it is submitted the right way.

do_now.text: Submit a supplemental claim every time demolition exposes damage that was not visible in the original scope.
do_now.why: This is the routine way a claim's scope grows — it is not treated as a new claim, but it does have its own reporting window under Fla. Stat. § 627.70132.

do_now.text: Keep every invoice and proof of payment for completed work.
do_now.why: Recoverable depreciation is released only against invoices for work already done.

do_now.text: Read the managed-repair or right-to-repair language in the policy before agreeing to the insurer's contractor.
do_now.why: Some policies allow declining the insurer's chosen contractor, and the choice can affect what gets paid.

do_now.text: Track the living-expense limit against the actual construction schedule and raise a shortfall in writing early if the rebuild will outrun the coverage.
do_now.why: Raising a shortfall early, in writing, creates a record before the money actually runs out.

never_do.text: Do not let demolition proceed without documenting newly exposed damage before it is covered back up.
never_do.consequence: Damage that is covered back up without documentation is effectively unprovable in a later supplement.

watch_for.signal: The insurer's own network contractor produces poor workmanship

documents: written request to raise the living-expense limit

title: If the answer is no, or not enough: the escalation ladder
plain_summary: Florida provides a specific sequence of steps, cheapest first. Each step remains available until a more expensive one is used.

do_now.text: Send a written demand to the adjuster, then the supervisor, laying the independent estimate against the insurer's line by line.
do_now.why: A written, line-item demand is the cheapest step and often the fastest to produce a change.

do_now.text: File a free complaint with the Florida Department of Financial Services Consumer Helpline (1-877-MY-FL-CFO).
do_now.why: It creates a regulatory record and often moves a stalled file on its own, at no cost.

do_now.text: Request DFS residential mediation.
do_now.why: The insurer pays for it, it is non-binding and confidential, and if the insurer never gave notice of this right, it loses its own ability to force appraisal instead.

do_now.text: Check whether the policy still has an appraisal clause before relying on it.
do_now.why: Some current Florida policies have removed the appraisal clause entirely, and filing suit first can waive it.

do_now.text: If hiring a public adjuster, check the license on the Department of Financial Services website first and confirm the fee is capped by law.
do_now.why: Florida caps a public adjuster's fee at 20 percent generally, or 10 percent for one year after a Governor-declared emergency, and nothing on money already paid before the contract was signed.

never_do.text: Do not refuse outright to cooperate with a legitimate examination under oath or a reasonable document request.
never_do.consequence: Refusing outright can be treated as a breach of the policy's cooperation clause and used as a defense to the entire claim.
never_do.reasonable_inaction: Declining to sign a blank, undated, unlimited financial authorization is always reasonable — cooperation does not require signing away an open-ended right to someone's financial history.

never_do.text: Do not file suit before serving the required pre-suit Notice of Intent.
never_do.consequence: A lawsuit filed without it is subject to dismissal regardless of the merits of the underlying claim.

watch_for.signal: An examination under oath is demanded, especially by outside counsel
A third adjuster is assigned within 60 days

documents: Notice of Intent to Initiate Litigation
